stories.headline: Fast, but never instant: what the speed of light really means
stories.summary: Light in a vacuum travels at exactly 299,792,458 metres per second, roughly a billion kilometres an hour. The figure is exact because, since 1983, the metre itself has been defined as the distance light travels in a vacuum in 1/299,792,458 of a second. Even at that speed, light from the Sun takes 8 minutes 19 seconds to reach the Earth.

stories.headline: Counting the bones of the adult skeleton
stories.summary: A newborn has around 270 bones. Many fuse together during growth, so an adult is left with around 206: 80 in the axial skeleton of skull, spine and rib cage, and 126 in the limbs and their girdles.

stories.headline: The laboratory beneath the Franco-Swiss border
stories.summary: CERN, established in 1954, is based in Meyrin, a western suburb of Geneva, on the France–Switzerland border. Its Large Hadron Collider runs through a 27 km circular tunnel located 100 metres underground. In 1989 the World Wide Web was invented there by Tim Berners-Lee.
